This report aims to create the following set of deliverables:

Data on how many clean energy projects have been categorically excluded vs. have required environmental assessments and environmental impact statements. Broken out by number of projects, generation capacity, and change over time.

Process Types by Energy Classification

Key Findings: Process Type

Clean energy projects use Categorical Exclusions at higher rates than fossil fuel or other types of projects. This could reflect smaller project footprints for clean energy projects? Fossil fuel projects show higher EA/EIS rates, consistent with larger environmental footprints requiring more detailed review.

Timeline Analysis for Clean Energy (In-progress)

Data Quality Notice

Timeline data cleaning is still in progress.

Focused on Categorical Exclusion (CEs) since they have the fewest dates and clearest timelines.

How timeline dates are extracted

  1. We start with the full text of each NEPA document and look for dates in various forms (e.g., “06/07/2018,” “July 7, 2010”, 13 Feb 2010).

  2. For each date we capture the surrounding sentence so we can understand why that date appears.

  3. Then we pass that through a fast classifier (BERT) that labels each date into one of four buckets:

    • Initiation: when the review appears to start (e.g., “Initiator Signature”, “application received,” or “initiation of consultation”)
    • Review: interim steps (e.g., Phase 1 was approved,” “review completed” or “interim review”)
    • Decision: final approval (e.g., “Approved by[Name], NEPA Compliance Officer”, “Authorizing Official”, Field Office Manager determination)
    • Other: when it doesn’t fall into one of those three buckets

  4. When no explicit initiation date is found, we use the earliest review date as a proxy for initiation.

Extraction Coverage (Full Run — CE Projects)

The BERT classifier was run on all 20,863 CE clean energy projects. Figure 4 visualizes the coverage rates. Decision dates are found for 83% of CE projects. Explicit initiation dates remain the biggest gap at 20%, though using the earliest review date as a proxy brings start-date coverage to 40%.

Figure 5 shows how many dates the classifier extracted per project. Most projects have 1–3 dates; projects with zero dates (4%) had extraction errors (e.g., no parseable text).

Figure 6 shows CE project counts by decision year.

Generation Capacity Analysis (In-progress)

Data Quality Notice

Generation capacity data cleaning is still in progress.

Key Findings: Capacity

Preliminary analysis shows that generation capacity data varies by review type and that EIS projects are predominantly utility-scale (>500 MW), while CE projects are mostly small-scale (<10 MW). This aligns with expectations: larger projects require more intensive environmental review.

To identify capacity generation, a regex-based extraction using pattern matching for values like “50 MW”, “1,500 megawatts”, “2.5 GW facility”. Capacity values normalized to MW for comparison.

Transmission-only projects account for 1,531 of 22,279 clean energy projects (6.9%) based on project_type tags (strict definition: only Electricity Transmission + Utilities).

Figure 7 shows that extraction rates vary significantly by process type. EIS projects have the highest coverage (81%), reflecting larger projects with explicit capacity documentation. CE projects have low coverage (8%) as expected—these are typically smaller projects that don’t require detailed capacity reporting.

Figure 8 shows the distribution of project sizes across process types. Among projects with extracted capacity:

  • EIS: 53% are utility-scale (>500 MW), median capacity of 538 MW
  • EA: Mixed distribution, median capacity of 60 MW
  • CE: 58% are small (<10 MW), median capacity of 1.2 MW

Example Project Extractions

A key challenge in capacity extraction is distinguishing the proposed project’s capacity from other numbers in the document (regional resource estimates, nearby facilities, energy consumption figures). The examples below show how the two-stage approach handles this.

Capacity-specific decisions to make:
  • Are the capacity bins (Small <10 MW, Medium 10–100 MW, Large 100–500 MW, Utility-scale >500 MW) appropriate?
  • Should we report the LLM-corrected values or flag cases where regex and LLM disagree for manual review?
  • How should we handle projects where no capacity is found — exclude from analysis or report as “not documented”?

Example A: EIS — Regional statistic vs. project capacity

Project: Fourmile Hill Geothermal Development Project

Method Value Unit Confidence Source text
Regex 4400.0 MW medium 1986 Northwest Conservation and Electric Power Plan (Power Plan), noted that "…approximately 4,400 megawatts of cost-...
LLM 49.9 MW high a 49.9-megawatt (MW) geothermal power plant.
Final (merged) 49.9 MW high —

Analysis: The regex extracted a large regional geothermal resource figure from the document’s background section. The LLM correctly identified the actual project capacity from the project description. The merged final value uses the LLM result.

Project: Sodium Test and Fill Facility

LLM 0.4 MW medium 0.4 megawatt

Example C: CE — Multiple equipment mentions

Project: Removal of C-Site Motor Generator (MG) Equipment

Method Value Unit Confidence Source text
Regex 350 kW low with asbestos insulation, and two condensers (6.5' long, 5' diameter each) * 350 KW diesel generator (non-operable ...
LLM 50 kW high 50 KW DC Generator
Final (merged) 50 kW high —

Analysis: This CE project involves removing equipment, so multiple capacity values appear in the document (different generators). The regex captured the largest value; the LLM identified the specific equipment being removed.

Next Steps for Generation Capacity

  1. Finalize capacity bins with client input on appropriate thresholds.
  2. Expand validation sample to confirm precision at scale.
  3. Review regex/LLM disagreements — the 78 cases where the two methods differ are the highest-priority candidates for manual review.
